rv.q: But the play is also a study in the overweening arrogance of a woman who, comparing herself to Anne, says “I am so much more than her” yet recklessly overplays her hand. The real surprise lies in the play’s portrait ofAnne.
Anne was unfortunate in many ways. She was afflicted by health problems that limited her mobility. She was pregnant 17 times but none of the children lived.

Romola Garai is Sarah Churchill, the queen’s haughty, beautiful, witty confidante. The enormously gifted wife to the great general the Duke of Marlborough (Chu Omambala), Sarah has come to take her childhood friendAnne for granted. Garai burns up the stage as Sarah, a gifted woman who might have been Prime Minister in another era.

Theatre Record 01 – 31 July 2017. There should be passion and pain here, though, as well as politics, but we don’t feel it. The play is two hours and 45 minutes and there are passages during which the attention drifts, as it does when you are reading a textbook, skimming through to miss out the dull bits.
